Senses.Explanation: Literally, “chasing the clod.” In the corpus it belongs to a recurrent animal comparison: “the lion bites the person; the hound chases the clod.” The phrase appears as an appraisal after exchanges and in admonitions such as “you must be a lion that bites the person; do not imitate the hound chasing the clod.” Related forms call people “mad dogs chasing the clod” and say “chasing the clod and tracking the scent does not yet make a good dog.” The headword occurs 326 times across 148 allowlisted texts.
Senses.Note: The hound and mad-dog variants share one literal image and one corpus deployment; they are not separate senses.

Occurrences.Kwic: 直須師子咬人，莫學韓獹逐塊
Occurrences.AttributionNote: The Complete Book of the Five Lamps, volumes 34–120 (五燈全書(第34卷-第120卷)): in Dawei Fabao's explicitly headed section, Dawei Fabao says one must be the lion that bites the person and must not imitate the Korean hound that chases the clod.

Connected Anthology of Verses on Old Chan Cases (禪宗頌古聯珠通集): the inline contributor note 大洪恩 assigns this verse to Chan master Dahong En, who contrasts the lion biting a person with the Korean hound chasing a clod.

Occurrences.Kwic: 師云：「獅子咬人，韓盧逐塊。」
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Recorded Sayings of Yushan (雨山和尚語錄): in public exchange, Yushan Shangsi appraises the monk with 'the lion bites the person; the Han hound chases the clod.'

Occurrences.Kwic: 如此等輩，皆是狂狗逐塊，何曾夢見有獅子奮迅的牙爪
Occurrences.AttributionNote: The Complete Book of the Five Lamps, volumes 34–120 (五燈全書(第34卷-第120卷)): in Kongxiang Gui's explicitly headed section, Kongxiang Gui calls the people just described mad dogs chasing clods and asks when they have ever dreamed of a lion's surging claws and fangs.
The Complete Book of the Five Lamps, volumes 34–120 (五燈全書(第34卷-第120卷)): in the same address, Kongxiang Gui says that chasing clods and following scent does not yet make a good dog.
